How much memory keeps the packets of the current session: for the Packets, Data and TLS tabs of a connection and for pcapng export and streaming.

When the buffer is full the oldest packets are dropped. Connections stay in the log; only their packets are gone.

Video and downloads fill it fastest. Fewer “Bytes per packet” (snaplen) fits many more packets into the same size.

How many bytes of each packet are kept. “Whole packet” keeps everything.\n\n128 bytes keep the headers only (addresses, ports, the start of TLS): enough to see who talks to whom, and the buffer then holds far more packets. The Data tab then shows only the beginning of each packet.

Packets are also written to pcapng files on the device, in a ring: when a file reaches its size or age a new one starts, and only the last N files are kept.\n\nThe files open in File analysis and in Wireshark. Without this switch nothing is written to disk; the buffer lives in memory only.

10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, link-local and multicast addresses are routed past the VPN: no filtering and no log for them.\n\nTurn it on if adb over Wi-Fi, casting to a TV or devices on your home network stop working while protection is on.

Packetwall can send traffic on to a SOCKS5 or HTTP CONNECT proxy, for example sing-box, v2rayNG or FlClash in “proxy only” mode. Only one VPN can be active, so this is how the two work together.

“All traffic”: everything allowed goes through the proxy. “Only rules with route via upstream”: only allow rules with the route "via upstream".

If the proxy app is on this phone, choose it as “Proxy app”: its own traffic then goes directly and does not loop.

HTTP CONNECT carries only TCP. SOCKS5 can carry UDP too (UDP ASSOCIATE), if the proxy supports it.\n\n“Block”: UDP that should go through the proxy is dropped; apps fall back to TCP (QUIC → HTTPS). “Send directly”: UDP bypasses the proxy and shows your real address.

Packetwall checks the proxy every few seconds.

Kill switch: while it is down, everything that should go through it is blocked, DNS included. Nothing leaks past the proxy.

Go directly: traffic goes out without the proxy until it comes back.

System DNS: apps ask the DNS server of the current network; Packetwall sees the names and answers blocked ones with 0.0.0.0.

Built-in DoH: Packetwall itself asks the chosen server over HTTPS. Your network does not see the names. With the upstream proxy, DoH goes through it.

Android's Private DNS hides names from the firewall. In Automatic mode Packetwall drops DoT and Android falls back to normal DNS. In the strict mode names are not visible: only rules by SNI work.

Drop: blocked packets just disappear. The app waits for a timeout, sometimes tens of seconds.\n\nReject: the app gets an immediate refusal (TCP RST, ICMP unreachable, NXDOMAIN for DNS) and gives up or tries something else at once. Pages and apps with blocked parts load faster.

Sets are checked from top to bottom, only enabled ones. The first set that has a rule for the connection decides; lower sets are not checked.

Within a set, the app's rules (and its groups') come before global ones, and the narrowest target wins: exact host > *.x > x with subdomains > IP/CIDR > country > everything. On a tie, block wins.

Example: “Allow example.com” in a higher set beats a blocklist below it.

A profile remembers which sets are on and in what order. Switching profiles switches sets, e.g. “Strict” for the night or “Work”.\n\nRules themselves live in sets and are shared by all profiles. Changes in the set list below edit the active profile.

Session: connections are kept in memory until protection is turned off.\n\n1–30 days: closed connections are saved to a database on the device and survive restarts; older ones are deleted. Packets are never saved there: for them use the packet buffer and writing to disk.

Blocklists come under their own licenses, shown on their pages.
Packetwall is free software under the GNU GPL 3.0 or later. The capture engine is based on PCAPdroid.
Tip: turn on “Always-on VPN” and “Block connections without VPN” for Packetwall, so no traffic goes around it while it is not running.

Packetwall runs a local VPN on the phone. Traffic does not go anywhere else: it passes through Packetwall right on the phone. Packetwall learns which app opened each connection and decides whether to let it through.\n\nNo root needed. While protection is on, another VPN cannot run: use the upstream proxy for that (below).

A rule is whose, where to and what to do. Whose: an app, an app group or everyone (a global rule). Where to: a domain (optionally with subdomains), an IP address or subnet, a country, an autonomous system (AS) or everything. What: block or allow; protocol and port can narrow it.\n\nThe quickest way to make a rule is from the Log: long press a connection.

Lists are community collections of domains: ads, trackers, malware. Each list is its own set with its own place in the priority.\n\nLists update by themselves. Your edits (entries turned off and added) are kept apart and applied after every update.
A group is several apps with shared rules, such as “Banks” or “Messengers”. A group rule applies to every member; the app\'s own rule beats the group\'s.

The log shows every connection: app, address, protocol, size and decision. Packets are kept in a memory buffer: view them, save them as pcapng, open them in Wireshark or stream them to a computer.\n\nPause stops the log and packets; the rules keep working.

So that no traffic goes around Packetwall while it is not running (after a reboot or a crash), turn on “Always-on VPN” and “Block connections without VPN” for Packetwall in Android settings.\n\nStrict Private DNS hides names: domain rules then work by SNI only.

While Packetwall is not running — after a reboot, an update or a crash — Android sends traffic directly, unfiltered.

In Android settings → Network & internet → VPN → Packetwall (⚙) turn on “Always-on VPN” and “Block connections without VPN”. Android then starts Packetwall itself and lets no traffic through while it is not running.

The interface and protection run in one process, so a rare interface crash also stops protection. With these two settings the internet just drops for a few seconds at that moment instead of going around.
